extracted.intended_audience: employers, policymakers, regulators, lawyers, worker advocates, and other stakeholders commenting on or implementing the FTC non-compete rule
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and explanation of alternative policy options to a categorical federal ban on non-competes (e.g., rebuttable presumption, disclosure, reporting, scope/duration limits, compensation requirements), with the Commission's findings and rationale for adopting or rejecting each alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: 120-day compliance period sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A 120-day compliance period gives employers sufficient time to identify workers with existing non-competes, determine which are senior executives, assess whether to maintain those non-competes, and revise employment policies/handbooks as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rationale: employers can assess which workers are senior executives and amend agreements; many workers subject to non-competes also have NDAs (95.6%); firms routinely complete onboarding in much shorter timeframes; small businesses have fewer workers and the senior-executive exclusion reduces burden; §910.3(b) preserves that the rule does not apply where the cause of action arose prior to the effective date, obviating need to extend compliance for pending litigation; uniform 120-day period eases implementation and complies with the Congressional Review Act (major rules may not take effect fewer than 60 days after publication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform 120-day effective date
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a single, uniform 120-day effective date for when the final rule goes into effect and when compliance is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission finds a uniform date reduces implementation burden and confusion; aligns with the 120-day compliance period and satisfies statutory timing constraints under the Congressional Review Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorical ban preferred over rebuttable presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: A categorical ban on non-competes is preferable to a rule implementing a rebuttable presumption of unlawfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: a rebuttable presumption would add complexity and uncertainty; undermine deterrence (employers would continue to impose non-competes unlikely to survive a presumption); increase litigation and compliance costs; produce in terrorem effects that chill worker mobility; shift burdens of proof in ways commentators found inappropriate; and be administratively burdensome compared with a categorical ban that more directly reduces prevalence and aggregate harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors proposed for a rebuttable-presumption test
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rebuttable presumption were used, commenters proposed focusing on particular factors to determine permissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed factors included: geographic scope and duration; presence and amount of liquidated damages or penalty provisions; whether the clause is narrowly tailored to prevent competition with actual competitors; the restrained worker's duties and income; availability of less restrictive alternatives; and the evidentiary burden (some suggested preponderance vs clear-and-convincing). Commission response: these factors were discussed but the Commission concluded a rebuttable presumption is not preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete alternatives involving rebuttable presumptions (Alternatives #1-#4) rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Four discrete alternatives involving categorical bans below/above thresholds and rebuttable presumptions were considered but rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives considered: #1 categorical ban below threshold/rebuttable presumption above; #2 categorical ban below threshold/no requirements above; #3 rebuttable presumption for all workers; #4 rebuttable presumption below threshold/no requirements above. Commission reasoned that rebuttable-presumption alternatives (Alts #1, #3, #4) raise the same concerns about uncertainty, in terrorem effects, litigation, and administrability, and thus are inferior to the adopted categorical approach. Alternative #2 (permitting non-competes above thresholds) was declined because such non-competes still negatively affect competitive conditions and exploit workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure rule alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Require employers to disclose the existence/terms of non-competes to workers prior to offer acceptance or by other timing rules (e.g., job ad, at offer, or at least five business days before signing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters: some argued disclosure increases worker awareness and bargaining; others said disclosure is often too late (presented on first day or after acceptance) and insufficient given take-it-or-leave-it dynamics. Evidence: the Starr, Prescott, and Bishara study shows correlations but not causation; Commission gave it little weight. Commission findings: disclosure would not address negative externalities non-competes impose on other workers, rivals, and consumers; would not remedy coercion due to bargaining imbalances; may modestly improve awareness but would not substantially reduce prevalence or aggregate harms; therefore Commission declines to adopt a disclosure rule. Suggested timing mechanisms and targeted disclosure (e.g., for sales of business) were considered but rejected as inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting rule alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Require employers to report information about their use of non-competes to the Commission (e.g., submit copies of non-compete agreements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential benefits: monitoring use, aiding enforcement, creating datasets for measuring compliance. Downsides: recurring significant compliance costs for employers, confidentiality concerns (exposing sensitive terms), and insufficient to meaningfully reduce prevalence or the competitive harms of non-competes. Commission therefore declines to adopt a reporting rule; some commenters proposed nullifying undisclosed agreements, but Commission did not adopt this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on scope and duration (bright-line or reasonableness) rejected
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives proposing bright-line geographic limits (e.g., 5, 10, 30 miles) or temporal limits (e.g., 6 months, 1–3 years), or a federal 'reasonableness' standard, were considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns: bright-line caps may become default maxima encouraging maximal restraints; reasonableness standards foster uncertainty similar to rebuttable presumptions; state laws already apply reasonableness in many places so a federal reasonableness standard would not mitigate current harms; even narrowed scope/duration still curtail mobility and produce spillover effects on new business formation and innovation; therefore Commission declines to adopt such limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation requirement alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit non-competes only if the worker receives separate compensation or a minimum level of consideration tied to the non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments for: modeled on some state laws (Massachusetts, Oregon) allowing non-competes with compensation. Commission reasons for rejection: compensation would not address negative externalities on other workers/consumers or aggregate harms (e.g., reduced job opportunities and innovation); in terrorem effects mean compensation may not produce genuine bargaining; administrability concerns and evasion risk (employers could suppress other wages or re-label compensation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of different alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine two or more alternatives (e.g., disclosure + limited duration + reporting) instead of a categorical ban.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission view: combinations might modulate some exploitative aspects but would lack the clarity and effectiveness of a comprehensive ban, would not sufficiently address aggregate/spillover harms, and therefore would fail to achieve the Commission's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-action alternative (reliance on existing law/case-by-case adjudication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decline to adopt a federal standard and rely instead on State laws and case-by-case litigation to address non-competes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments: some support relying on existing state frameworks to allow individualized fact-sensitive outcomes and state-level experimentation; others highlighted patchwork law, uncertainty about reasonableness tests, cross-border complications with remote/hybrid work, and difficulty predicting outcomes. Commission finds that case-by-case adjudication and existing law alone would not address aggregate harms, enforcement costs, or provide clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking preferred over adjudication when harms are aggregate and widespread
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulemaking is the appropriate method to address non-competes when harms arise from widespread, aggregate use across labor markets and product/service markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rationale: prevalence of non-competes (estimated 2.92 million firms using them) and scale of harms make rulemaking more efficient than piecemeal litigation; rulemaking provides clearer notice of obligations under Section 5, simplifies enforcement by streamlining proof required, avoids slow and costly adjudication against many firms, and better addresses harms that operate in the aggregate (e.g., suppressed wages, reduced new business formation, inhibited innovation). The Supreme Court recognizes agency discretion to choose rulemaking over adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior executive and business-sale exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of allowing non-competes for senior executives or in the context of sales of a business entity as limited exceptions to a categorical ban.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments urged exceptions for senior/highly-paid workers and sales of businesses. Commission addressed these comments elsewhere (Parts IV.C, V.D.1, V.A) and limited existing-noncompetes exception for senior executives in the final rule; for sales of a business, Commission concluded a disclosure rule is unnecessary given bargaining power in sales transactions and lack of evidence of deceptive practices in that context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small business compliance considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether small businesses have sufficient time and resources to comply with the final rule and whether regulatory design reduces their burdens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission findings: 120-day compliance period is sufficient for small businesses because they have fewer workers; exclusion for existing non-competes for senior executives relieves burden for firms that use non-competes only with those workers; Commission adopted §910.2(b) modifications to reduce compliance burdens and simplify compliance for small businesses.
